title: Summary and review exercise
competency: Bring together the ideas of Unit 3.

keywords.def: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
A pure substance of two or more elements chemically combined.
The combining power of an element. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.
A shorthand expression of a chemical reaction through symbols and formulas.

en.text: Elements have symbols; compounds have formulas. Valence is the combining power and gives formulas by criss-cross. In a reaction, reactants become products. Mass is conserved, so equations must be balanced by changing coefficients only.

screens.title: Unit summary
paras: An atomic symbol is a shorthand way of representing elements.
A compound is a pure substance of two or more elements chemically combined.
A chemical formula is the symbolic representation of an element or a compound.
A molecule is the smallest particle with a stable, independent existence.

screens.title: Unit summary (continued)
paras: The combining power of an element is called valence. Most have valence 1, 2 or 3.
A polyatomic ion is a charged group of atoms.
In a reaction, reactants change into new substances called products.
Signs of a reaction: colour change, gas, heat change, precipitate.
Matter is neither created nor destroyed. Equations are balanced by inspection or the LCM method.

children.label: Elements
children.info: Pure substances written with symbols, like Fe and Na. Some are diatomic, like O₂ and N₂.

children.label: Symbols
children.info: A shorthand for an element: a capital letter, sometimes with a small letter (He, Cu).

children.label: Compounds
children.info: Two or more elements chemically combined, like H₂O and NaCl.

children.label: Valence and formulas
children.info: Valence is the combining power. Criss-cross the valences to write a formula: Fe(III) + Cl → FeCl₃.

children.label: Chemical reactions
children.info: Reactants change into new substances called products.

children.label: Signs
children.info: Colour change, gas given off, temperature change, precipitate.

children.label: Conservation of mass
children.info: Matter is neither created nor destroyed.

children.label: Balancing
children.info: Change coefficients only, by inspection or by the LCM method.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
A pure substance of two or more elements chemically combined.
The combining power of an element. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.
A shorthand expression of a chemical reaction through symbols and formulas.

screens.why:
Na is the symbol of sodium (Natrium).
NO₃⁻ is the nitrate ion, a polyatomic ion.
CaCl₂ is calcium chloride.
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO is the burning of magnesium.
screens.text: Match each symbol, formula or equation to its meaning.
Symbols and formulas: true or false? The formula and symbol of nitrogen are the same.
screens.why:
The symbol of nitrogen is N: one atom.
Nitrogen gas is diatomic, so its formula is N₂.
N and N₂ are not the same.
So the statement is false.

screens.text: Writing formulas: what is the chemical formula of iron (III) chloride?
screens.why:
Iron (III) means iron has valence 3.
Chlorine has valence 1.
Criss-cross: Fe₁Cl₃.
So iron (III) chloride is FeCl₃.
FeCl₂ is iron (II) chloride.

screens.text: Challenge, write and balance: aluminum + bromine → aluminum bromide
screens.why:
Formulas: Al (valence 3) and Br (valence 1) give AlBr₃. Bromine gas is Br₂.
Al + Br₂ → AlBr₃.
Br: 2 on the left, 3 on the right. LCM of 2 and 3 is 6.
So 3Br₂ and 2AlBr₃. Then Al: 2 on the right, so 2Al.
2Al + 3Br₂ → 2AlBr₃. Check: Al 2 = 2, Br 6 = 6.
screens.clue: Write formulas first; bromine is diatomic.

items.text: Review Exercise 1, true or false: a compound is a pure substance.
items.why:
A compound has a fixed make-up of elements.
Its elements are chemically combined.
So a compound is a pure substance: True.

items.text: Review Exercise 2, true or false: in a chemical reaction atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
items.why:
Atoms only rearrange in a reaction.
They are never made and never lost.
This is the law of conservation of mass: True.

items.text: Review Exercise 3, true or false: O₂ and 2O have the same meaning.
items.why:
O₂ is one molecule: two oxygen atoms joined.
2O is two separate oxygen atoms.
The subscript joins atoms. The coefficient counts separate units.
So they do not mean the same: False.

items.text: Review Exercise 4, true or false: the symbol of copper is Co.
items.why:
Copper's symbol comes from its Latin name, Cuprum.
So copper is Cu.
Co is the symbol of cobalt.
The statement is false.

items.text: Review Exercise 6, true or false: respiration is a chemical change.
items.why:
Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
The products are new substances.
So respiration is a chemical change: True.

items.text: Latin names: what is the Latin name of silver?
items.why:
Silver's Latin name is Argentum, so its symbol is Ag.
Kalium is potassium (K).
Natrium is sodium (Na).
Cuprum is copper (Cu).

items.text: Diatomic molecules: all of these can exist as diatomic molecules EXCEPT
items.why:
Hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine exist as H₂, O₂ and Cl₂.
Sodium is a metal.
It is written Na, not as a pair of atoms.
So sodium is the exception.

items.text: Symbols: what is the chemical symbol for helium?
items.why:
A symbol starts with a capital letter.
A second letter is always small.
H is hydrogen, so helium needs two letters: He.
HE has two capitals, which is never written.

Zinc is Zn. Phosphorus is P. Calcium is Ca.
Mercury is Hg, from its Latin name Hydrargyrum.
Tin is Sn, from its Latin name Stannum.
items.text: Review Exercise 18: match each element to its symbol.
Review Exercise 19 b, balance: NH₃ + O₂ → NO + H₂O
items.why:
H: 3 in NH₃, 2 in H₂O. Use 2NH₃ and 3H₂O (6 H).
N: 2 on the left, so 2NO.
O: right 2 + 3 = 5, so 5/2 O₂. A half is not allowed.
Double everything: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O.
Check: N 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 10 = 4 + 6.
items.clue: Balance H, then N, then O; clear 5/2.
